title: The Natural Diamond Price List
kicker: Every shape, every weight, trade and retail side by side
standfirst: What a natural diamond actually costs — the wholesale benchmark the trade pays, the asking price the counter shows, and the spread between them, across ten shapes and eleven weight bands. Every figure is dated, every source is named, and every number we modelled rather than observed says so.

weights.caption: Trade against retail, per carat and per stone
weights.sub: Trade column is the IDEX price-driver average where a driver exists, RAPI where it does not. Retail is the observed five-retailer median at one carat and a declining multiple of the trade benchmark elsewhere — stated, not hidden.
weights.withheld_note: The 4.00-4.99 ct band is the one figure on this page we decline to print. IDEX carries it at $32,277 a carat — above the five-carat band at $21,449 — on a thin slice of the market. A four-carat stone does not cost more per carat than a five-carat stone. The band is too thin to mean anything, so it stays blank rather than being smoothed into something that looks like a price.
weights.ten_note: No public source publishes a wholesale per-carat figure for ten carats. IDEX carries no driver at that weight, RAPI publishes no level, and the independent Antwerp grids stop at six. The ten-carat line is a live retail asking average and is marked as such.

dual_basis.caption: Why there are two trade numbers
dual_basis.sub: RAPI reads the top of the market; IDEX reads the middle of it. Where both exist they disagree, and the gap is the point.
dual_basis.note: RAPI is the average asking price of the ten per cent lowest-priced D–H, IF–VS2, GIA-graded stones on RapNet. It is a floor for a narrow top specification, not a market mean. IDEX price drivers average a far broader spread of colour and clarity. At one carat the broad market sits 22.1% below the narrow top spec (3,019 / 3,876 = 77.9% of it), which is what you would expect — and a useful reminder that a single 'diamond price' does not exist.
dual_basis.asof: RAPI at its newest published point, 2026-10-25 - IDEX price drivers read 2026-10-26

colour.caption: Colour
colour.sub: D to K, one carat round, VS1 — index and applied retail asking
colour.note: A K costs 62.5% less per carat than a D at the same weight, shape and clarity. An independent Antwerp grid puts the same swing at 61.6% — close enough, from a different desk, to trust the shape of the curve.

clarity.caption: Clarity
clarity.sub: IF to SI2, one carat round, G colour — index and applied retail asking
clarity.note: SI2 costs 59.6% less than IF. The two grades that matter most to a buyer's wallet are the ones nobody can see: the step from VS2 to SI1 costs 17% and is invisible to the eye in most stones.

matrix_note: We publish colour and clarity as two separate ladders, never crossed into a grid. Multiplying one by the other would reconstruct a proprietary price list cell by cell, and that list is somebody else's copyrighted product. The ladders are drawn from published index aggregates; the grid is not ours to print.

shapes.caption: Shape
shapes.sub: Ten cuts, one carat, against the round brilliant — live asking prices, 169,324 stones

tiers.name: The round
tiers.why: Roughly a third of rough is lost cutting one. You pay for the waste.

tiers.name: Elongated brilliants
tiers.why: Oval, pear, marquise. Cut with the grain of the rough, so less is thrown away — and they look larger face-up than their weight.

tiers.name: Step cuts and squares
tiers.why: Emerald, asscher, radiant, princess, cushion, heart. Cheapest per carat, and the least forgiving: an open table shows every inclusion the round would have hidden.

shapes.conflict_note: Pear and marquise are the two shapes we will not price to a single number. Live inventory at one house puts pear 44% below its own round; another retailer's published differential puts it 18.7% above. That is not rounding — it is two different books. Read the shape tier, not the decimal.

spread.caption: The spread
spread.sub: How much the counter adds, by weight
spread.note: Markup falls as the stone grows. A third of a carat carries roughly double the trade price; a five-carat carries about a third on top. The small stone pays for the shop.

retailers.caption: The same stone, five counters
retailers.sub: 1.00 ct round, G, VS1 — asking price per carat, observed 2026-07-30. James Allen removed 2026-09-15: it has been folded into Blue Nile and no longer trades as an independent retailer (jamesallen.com/loose-diamonds/round-cut-diamonds/ 301-redirects to bluenile.com/?jaRedirect=true, confirmed by the chief 2026-09-09).
retailers.note: A 2.19× spread on an identical grading report, five counters now that James Allen is off the list (it was folded into Blue Nile, confirmed 2026-09-09). This is not error and it is not all margin — most of it is cut. The bottom of the range is a stone graded G VS1 and cut to a commercial standard; the top is the same paper cut to a super-ideal tolerance. The certificate does not price the diamond. The cut does.

magic.caption: The magic weights
magic.sub: What crossing a round number costs

rows.note: Like for like, same colour and clarity. Four independent methods converge inside a single point.
Per carat, on the IDEX drivers. Double the weight, nearly triple the rate.

magic.note: Buy 0.90 and nobody at the table can tell. That is the single cheapest piece of advice on this page.
magic.band_caveat: Divide the 1.00 ct row of the main table by the 0.90 ct row and you get +60%, not +24%. Both are right and they measure different things. The main table averages every stone inside a weight band, and the specification mix changes as the bands rise — more of the better colours sit above a carat. The +23 to +24% here is the same colour and the same clarity on both sides of the line. That figure is the one to plan a purchase around.

lab.caption: Against lab-grown
lab.sub: Where the two markets now sit

rows.k: 1 ct round, natural, live retail average
1 ct round, lab-grown, live retail average

lab.inversion: The fancy-shape discount has inverted in lab-grown. Where a natural oval costs 23% less than a natural round, a lab oval costs 11% more than a lab round — and a lab princess costs 23% more. In a market with no scarcity, price follows growing time and cutting loss rather than rarity, and the ranking flips. It is the cleanest single illustration of what the two markets actually are.
lab.followup: A full lab-grown list follows this one.

rows.b: De Beers realised $110 a carat in the second quarter of 2026, down 37% year on year; $105 across the half, down 32%. Its half-year price index reads 69, off 16%. The full-year 2025 average was $142.

rows.h: Polished has stopped falling at the bottom
rows.b: RAPI at 0.30 ct reads $927.08 at its 2026-10-25 point against $845.11 on 1 January, up 9.7% on the year, and sits 12.4% under its $1,057.85 level of 1 September 2025. The small-stone recovery is the only weight band on this page that is higher than it started the year.

One carat reads $3,876.42 at its 2026-10-25 point against $4,125.20 on 1 January, down 6.0% on the year, and 12.9% under its $4,448.65 level of 1 September 2025. Three carat reads $18,264.96 against $18,225.61, up 0.2% on the year.
US duty effective 24 July 2026: India 10%, EU zero, Hong Kong and China 12.5% plus Section 301. Canada goes to 50% from 19 August.

rows.h: Sanctions bite at half a carat
rows.b: The G7 threshold on Russian-origin stones has stood at 0.50 ct since 1 September 2024, and a due-diligence statement has been required on polished imports since 1 January 2026.

rows.h: Fancy colour is flat, not falling
rows.b: The Fancy Colour Research Foundation index was −0.2% on the quarter and −0.9% on the year in Q1 2026. Blue is best read as unchanged: two houses reported the same release as +0.3% and −0.3%.

rows.h: The top of the market is fine
rows.b: Gem Diamonds averaged $1,395 a carat in the first half, up 38%, with a 52.24 ct white at $32,908 a carat. At auction the Ocean Dream, 5.5 ct vivid blue-green, made $17.3m — about $3.15m a carat.

rows.h: And De Beers is changing hands
rows.b: The Gareth Penny consortium is reported at about $1bn for Anglo American's 85%, against a book value near $2.3bn earlier this year.

The trade per-carat column at 0.50, 0.70, 0.90, 1.00, 1.50, 2.00, 3.00 and 5.00 carats is read directly from IDEX price drivers on 2026-10-26. The 0.30 ct figure is RAPI at its own newest published point, 2026-10-25. The one-carat retail figure is the median of five retailers priced on 30 July 2026 (James Allen was dropped 2026-09-15, folded into Blue Nile). The shape table is a live sample of 169,324 asking prices. The colour and clarity indices are published aggregates at 31 December 2025.

Retail per carat at every weight other than one carat. It is the trade benchmark multiplied by a factor that falls from 2.10 at 0.30 ct to 1.35 at 5.00 ct, calibrated on the observed 1.84 at one carat and cross-checked against the disclosed gross margins of three listed retailers. Rows carrying modelled figures say so in the table.

The 4.00–4.99 ct band, because its published per-carat average exceeds the band above it on a sample of 0.32%. And the colour × clarity grid, because building one from published premiums would reconstruct a copyrighted price list.

All figures are US dollars per carat unless a whole-stone column says otherwise. Rapaport's index documentation describes its levels in hundreds of dollars per carat; at that reading a one-carat stone would price near $388,000. The levels are only coherent as plain dollars per carat and are printed here as such.
This is a market reference, not a valuation and not an offer. Every stone prices on its own certificate, its own cut and its own day.
